sections.html:
Chandler sits in the East Valley, roughly 22 miles southeast of downtown Phoenix, and ranks fourth in population among Arizona cities with 278,748 people as of July 1, 2025. Two thirds of homes (65.0%) are lived in by their owners. The median owner-occupied home is worth $507,800, owners with a mortgage pay a median $2,044 a month, and median gross rent is $1,902.

Turnover is low. About 86.6% of residents were in the same house a year earlier, so the comparison sales a buyer can find near you will be few.

Loop 202 (the Santan Freeway) and Loop 101 (the Price Freeway) carve the city into North, West and South Chandler. People shop by freeway access and by the nearest park, Tumbleweed Park for example, so put both in your listing text.

Anything built under a permit needs a closed permit, and Chandler says missing ones tend to surface at sale time. The Development Services homeowner manual describes what can follow: a Legal Notice, an Order to Comply and permit fees charged at double. The city can order non-compliant work, a room addition for example, torn out on the owner's dime. A buyer with an FHA loan hits another wall, since that program will not lend when county assessor records disagree with the house.

Some projects need no permit:

  • One-story detached accessory structures up to 120 square feet and 7 feet high
  • Fences not over 7 feet high
  • Retaining walls not over 4 feet high, unless they support a surcharge

Type the street address into the city's online development permits portal to read the permit history. For questions, reach the Plan Reviewer of the Day at 480-782-3078 or prod@chandleraz.gov. An HOA subdivision adds a second layer: the city does not enforce HOA rules, so approvals from the association are your responsibility.

To legalize something before closing, go to the Development Services permit counter at 215 East Buffalo Street in downtown Chandler. The minimum permit fee is $60 for a valuation of $500 or less and climbs with the value of the work, and plan review fees are due the day you submit plans.

sections.h2: Fix the paperwork or sell as is?
sections.html:
A hole in the permit file rarely kills a sale, yet it moves money between you and the buyer. Run the address yourself first. An open permit or a missing final inspection leaves three paths: close it out, accept a lower price, or find a buyer fine with the gap.

Cash buyers generally take a house as it stands, so no repair list, staged showings or lender appraisal sit between you and the closing table. A retail buyer with a mortgage brings an inspector and an underwriter who both read the file closely. Weigh the cost of fixing the paperwork against your calendar before you commit to either route.

Maricopa County bills Chandler property in two installments. Arizona fixes the dates, so they repeat every year.

InstallmentDue dateLate after
First halfOctober 15 p.m., November 1
Second halfMarch 15 p.m., May 1

Paying the whole year by December 31 avoids interest. Tell your escrow officer where your payments stand when escrow opens, so the closing statement divides the year the right way. The county Treasurer's calendar shows any date that slides because of a weekend.

One more check for former rentals: when a rental registration is on file, the Maricopa County Assessor lists the parcel type as Residential/Rental.

The Maricopa County Recorder records a Chandler deed for $30 a document. It takes the deed only with an affidavit of property value or an exemption code written on it, and its staff cannot tell you which code applies, so ask the title company or an attorney.

The office is at 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200, Phoenix, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. If you mail originals, expect them back in two to four weeks. By A.R.S. 11-1133 the affidavit carries the price, date, legal description and parcel number, and A.R.S. 11-1134 names the transfers that are exempt. Escrow files all of this for you. What it needs from you are correct names, the parcel number and a phone number that works on closing day.

A house rented, advertised or offered on a web-based platform is a short-term rental in Chandler, however long the guest stays. Each rental location needs a city license under Chapter 22 of the City Code.

The owner's checklist:

  • The state's Transaction Privilege Tax license
  • County rental registration through Maricopa County
  • Notice to neighbors
  • The city license application
  • Emergency contact information posted inside the unit
  • State and city license numbers shown in every advertisement

The license runs to June 30 each year, and approval normally takes seven business days. A written notice starts a 30 day clock, and an owner who still has not applied can face a civil penalty of up to $1,000 per month. The city lists a combined short-term rental tax rate of 11.67%, made up of 4.40% Chandler and 7.27% state.

If your house has been a rental, call the city's Tax and License office to find out what happens to the license at sale.

After you say yes to an offer, a title company opens escrow. Its officer searches for liens, requests payoff letters from your lender, divides the year's property tax between the two sides, and passes the deed and affidavit to the Maricopa County Recorder. You sign, the buyer's money arrives, and the deed gets recorded. With a cash buyer no underwriter reviews the file, so the calendar can shrink to a few weeks. A loan-backed purchase waits on underwriting.

Two snags show up late. A permit that was never finaled can stall a financed sale at the final hour, and an unpaid half of the tax bill comes out of your proceeds at the table. Clear both early.

Occupied or inherited houses need a possession date in writing. Ask the buyer whether belongings may stay or the rooms must be empty.

Start one folder with the parcel number, newest tax bill, HOA contact, repair notes and permit records. A buyer who reads it can price your house without a round of emails. Say early if the house is empty, inherited or rented out, since closing runs differently for each.

Lay any written offer next to what a listing would net once repairs, carrying costs and slow weeks are subtracted. Then read the entire agreement before signing.

faqs.q: How many people live in Chandler?
faqs.a: The population is 278,748 as of July 1, 2025, up from 275,987 counted in the 2020 census. Chandler is the fourth most populous city in Arizona.

faqs.q: Does Chandler require a permit for a room addition?
faqs.a: Yes. Remodeling needs a permit unless the work is on the city's exempt list. Call the Plan Reviewer of the Day at 480-782-3078 before you start, or if you are unsure about work a previous owner did.

faqs.q: What is the Maricopa County recording fee for a deed?
faqs.a: The standard fee is $30 per document. The deed must also carry an affidavit of property value or an exemption code.

faqs.q: Do I need a license to rent my Chandler house short term?
faqs.a: Yes. Each rental location needs a city short-term rental license, plus a state Transaction Privilege Tax license and county rental registration. Operating without one can draw a civil penalty of up to $1,000 per month.

faqs.q: When do Maricopa County property taxes go delinquent?
faqs.a: The first half is delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 1 and the second half after 5 p.m. on May 1. Full-year taxes can be paid through December 31 without interest.
